pairs.rationale: Both introduce the disciples' question or dispute about which of them is greatest. Matthew names greatness in the kingdom of the heavens.
Both have Jesus place a child among the disciples as part of His answer about greatness. Mark also describes Him embracing the child.
Both make becoming or receiving like a child necessary for entering God's kingdom. Matthew says to turn and become like children; Mark speaks of receiving the kingdom like a child.
Matthew identifies the person humbling himself like the child as greatest; Luke concludes the child-reception teaching by calling the least among the disciples great.
Both say that receiving such a child in Jesus' name is receiving Jesus Himself. Mark extends the chain of reception to the One who sent Him.
Both warn against causing a believing little one to stumble and compare the offender's fate unfavorably with being thrown into the sea wearing a millstone.
Both acknowledge the unavoidable coming of stumbling blocks while pronouncing woe on the person through whom they come. Necessity does not remove that person's responsibility.

Both use cutting off a stumbling hand or foot to contrast entering life maimed with retaining the members and entering fire. Mark's original consecutive units here are 43 and 45; absent verse 44 is not invented.
Both use removing a stumbling eye to contrast one-eyed life with retaining two eyes and entering Gehenna. Mark continues with undying worm and unextinguished fire.

Matthew grounds protection of little ones in their angels' access to the Father; Hebrews describes angels serving heirs of salvation. Both associate angels with care for God's people; Hebrews does not repeat the face-of-the-Father claim.
Both tell of a shepherd with a hundred sheep who leaves ninety-nine to seek the missing one. Matthew locates the ninety-nine on mountains; Luke places them in the wilderness.
Both emphasize exceptional joy when the lost sheep is found and compare it with the ninety-nine. Luke develops the image into heavenly joy over a repentant sinner.
Matthew applies the lost-sheep story to the Father's will that no little one perish; Luke applies it to heavenly joy over one repentant sinner. Both emphasize the recovery of the one.
Both require rebuking a sinning brother and seeking restoration. Matthew specifies private correction and gaining the brother; Luke explicitly connects repentance and forgiveness.
The requirement to establish every matter upon two or three witnesses closely repeats Deuteronomy's rule. Matthew applies it after unsuccessful private correction.

Both describe limiting fellowship with someone inside the community who persists in wrongdoing. Paul specifies offenses and exclusion from association; Matthew describes refusal to hear and treatment as an outsider.

The earlier saying to Peter uses the same earthly binding and loosing with heavenly correspondence. Matthew 18 addresses the disciples amid communal discipline rather than repeating the promise of keys.
Both connect requests with the Father's giving. Matthew 18 specifies two disciples agreeing on a request; the Sermon supplies the broader assurance of good gifts to those who ask.
Both promise Jesus' continuing presence with disciples. Matthew 18 specifies gathering in His name; the conclusion promises His presence throughout the days until the age's completion.
Peter asks about forgiving a brother repeatedly, up to seven times; Luke describes seven sins in a day with repeated repentance and forgiveness.
Both reject repeated sin as a reason to stop forgiveness. Matthew answers seventy times seven; Luke describes seven occurrences in a day and explicitly specifies repentance.
Both parables introduce a ruler calling slaves to an accounting. Matthew's king settles debts; Luke's returning king asks what business entrusted money produced. They are different parables.
Both parables use indebtedness and inability to repay to introduce forgiveness. Matthew specifies ten thousand talents; Luke contrasts five-hundred-denarius and fifty-denarius debts.
Both depict an unpaid debt threatening enslavement of the debtor's children. Matthew includes the debtor and wife in the threatened sale; the widow in Kings reports a lender coming for her sons.
This explicitly same-chapter comparison repeats the request for patience and promise to repay. The first slave's plea becomes his fellow slave's plea to him, exposing his inconsistency.
Both describe a creditor canceling debt for someone unable to repay. Matthew attributes the release to compassion; Luke's cancellation introduces a question about grateful love.

The same parable contrasts this violently demanded hundred-denarius debt with the ten-thousand-talent debt previously owed by the demanding slave himself. The differing amounts expose the reversal of mercy.
This same-chapter plea mirrors the slave's earlier request for patience and promise to repay. He now hears essentially the request he made to his master.
The same chapter contrasts the master's compassionate release with the forgiven slave's refusal of patience and imprisonment of his fellow debtor.
The master explicitly recalls his earlier cancellation of the slave's debt. This same-chapter callback identifies the mercy already received that makes the slave's behavior culpable.
The master demands mercy patterned on his own mercy; Luke calls disciples to be merciful as their Father is merciful. Luke states the principle directly instead of through this debt parable.
The merciless slave faces judgment for withholding mercy, corresponding to James's warning of judgment without mercy for someone showing none. James does not repeat the torture or debt imagery.
Both connect the Father's treatment with the person's forgiveness of others. Matthew 18 adds from the heart and applies the principle through the unforgiving-slave parable.
Both locate Jesus' movement in Judea and beyond the Jordan after leaving the prior setting. Matthew explicitly says He departed from Galilee.
Both describe great crowds coming to Jesus and His healing them. This is a recurring crowd-healing pattern in different narrative settings, not a claim that the occasions are one event.
Both have Pharisees test Jesus by questioning the lawfulness of divorcing a wife. Matthew explicitly adds for any cause.
The appeal to the Creator making them male and female recalls Genesis's creation of humanity as male and female in God's image, here invoked in the divorce dispute.
Matthew quotes leaving father and mother, union with the wife, and the two becoming one flesh. The source wording remains distinct, including cleave versus be joined.
Both conclude that the married pair are no longer two but one flesh and prohibit humans from separating what God has yoked together.
Both opponents appeal to Moses and a divorce certificate. Matthew calls their objection a command; Mark's speakers call it permission to write a certificate and dismiss the wife.
Both explain the Mosaic divorce provision by hardness of heart and contrast it with creation's beginning. Matthew explicitly calls it permission and denies that it was originally so.
Both associate divorce followed by remarriage with adultery. Matthew includes a sexual-immorality exception absent here from Mark, who additionally discusses a wife divorcing her husband.
Jesus says the saying can be received only by those to whom it is given; Paul acknowledges differing gifts from God while discussing marriage and remaining unmarried.

Matthew includes eunuchs for the kingdom among distinct categories; Paul emphasizes unmarried people's undistracted devotion to the Lord. The comparison concerns kingdom-oriented renunciation, without making Paul repeat Matthew's three categories.
Both describe children being brought for Jesus' touch or blessing and the disciples rebuking them. Matthew mentions laying on hands and prayer.
Both forbid hindering the children and say the kingdom belongs to such as these. Mark also records Jesus' indignation at the disciples' interference.
Both describe Jesus laying His hands on the children. Mark adds embracing and blessing; Matthew then narrates His departure.
Both introduce a man's question about obtaining or inheriting eternal life. Mark's man addresses Good Teacher; Matthew's man asks what good thing to do.
Both address goodness and the commandments. Matthew asks why the man asks about what is good; Mark asks why he calls Jesus good and names God as the One who is good.
Both list prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft, and false witness in the reply about eternal life. Mark also includes do not defraud.
Both include honoring father and mother in the list. Matthew additionally gives love of neighbor here, a clause absent from this verse of Mark's list.
Both have the questioner assert that he has kept the listed commandments. Matthew adds what remains lacking; Mark says he has kept them from youth.
Both require selling possessions, giving to the poor, and following Jesus, promising heavenly treasure. Matthew frames it as wishing to be perfect; Mark says the man lacks one thing.
Both say the man left grieved because he possessed much. Matthew describes many properties; Mark adds his fallen expression at the saying.
Both have Jesus address the disciples about a wealthy person's difficulty entering God's kingdom after the man's departure.
Both compare a camel passing through a needle's opening with a rich person's entrance into God's kingdom. Neither supplied verse identifies a city gate.
Both describe the disciples' extreme astonishment and question about who can be saved after the teaching concerning wealth.
Both answer the salvation question by contrasting human impossibility with God's ability and explicitly say all things are possible with God.
Both have Peter say the disciples left everything and followed Jesus. Matthew also asks what then will be theirs.
Both promise faithful followers thrones and a role judging Israel's twelve tribes. Matthew specifies twelve thrones and the regeneration; Luke connects the promise with Jesus' kingdom table.
Both promise a hundredfold and eternal life to those leaving family or property for Jesus. Mark distinguishes present reception with persecutions from eternal life in the coming age.
Both close the teaching on possessions and discipleship with the reversal that many first will be last and the last first.
The kingdom parable follows the first-and-last saying and repeats it at 20:16. This same-book framing link identifies the parable's context, not an independent account of the vineyard hiring.
The parable begins with an agreed day's wage. Deuteronomy supplies the legal background of paid labor and wages due that day, but does not prescribe the one-denarius amount.

The owner promises hired workers whatever is just; Colossians requires authorities over labor to provide what is just and equitable. Colossians addresses masters and slaves rather than daily hired workers.
The owner orders payment at evening. Leviticus forbids keeping a hired worker's wages overnight; the shared point is paying rather than detaining the worker's wages until morning.

This same-chapter comparison shows even the last-hired workers receiving the denarius agreed with the first workers for the full day. The repeated amount establishes the surprising equality of payment.

The same chapter gives the eleventh-hour workers and the first workers a denarius each. The repeated payment contrasts the first workers' expectation of more with the equal amount actually distributed.

The early workers resent generous treatment of latecomers, comparable to the older son's anger at his father's welcome of the returning brother. These are different parables about resentment of another's benefit.

Both complaints contrast long service with favorable treatment of someone considered less deserving. The workers cite the day's heat; the older son cites years of obedience before the brother's feast.
The householder explicitly recalls the same chapter's original denarius agreement. That earlier contract supplies the stated basis for denying that the first worker has been wronged.

Both householder and father defend generosity toward the late or returning recipient while answering a resentful earlier claimant. The father cites the brother's restoration rather than a wage contract.

Both use an evil eye in a monetary setting to expose begrudging another's benefit. Deuteronomy warns against withholding help from a poor brother; Matthew rebukes envy of the owner's generosity, a different financial situation.
Both state the first-and-last reversal. Matthew concludes the worker parable; Mark places the saying at the end of the preceding teaching on discipleship and possessions.
Both set the passion prediction on the road up to Jerusalem and have Jesus take the Twelve aside. Mark adds the followers' astonishment and fear.
Both predict betrayal of the Son of Man to chief priests and scribes, who will condemn Him to death, during the Jerusalem journey.
Both predict Gentile abuse, flogging, death, and resurrection. Matthew names crucifixion and on the third day; Mark says they will kill Him and He will rise after three days.
Both introduce a request associated with Zebedee's sons. Matthew has their mother approach with them and ask; Mark reports James and John themselves making the request.
Both have Jesus ask what is wanted and hear a request for seats at His right and left. Matthew names the kingdom and the mother speaks; Mark names glory and the sons speak.
Both challenge the requesters with drinking Jesus' cup and record their claim that they can. Mark also includes a baptism image absent from Matthew's supplied verse.
Both affirm sharing Jesus' cup but assign the right and left seats to those for whom they are prepared. Matthew explicitly names the Father as their preparer.
Both describe the ten becoming indignant with James and John after hearing the request for privileged places. Matthew calls them the two brothers.
Both contrast the disciples' community with rulers of nations lording it over others and great ones exercising authority over them.
Both reject domination among disciples and define becoming great in their community through becoming a servant.
Both define the desire to be first through slavery or service to others. Mark says slave of all; Matthew says your slave.
Both ground servant leadership in the Son of Man coming to serve rather than be served and giving His life as a ransom for many.
Both place the blind-healing narrative as Jesus leaves Jericho with a considerable crowd. Mark also names the blind beggar Bartimaeus.
Both have roadside blind petitioners invoke Jesus as Son of David and ask mercy. Matthew depicts two blind men; Mark centers on the named Bartimaeus.
Both have crowds attempt to silence blind petitioners, who then cry for the Son of David's mercy more loudly. Matthew has two men; Mark narrates one.
Both have Jesus stop, call the blind petitioner or petitioners, and ask what they want Him to do. Mark elaborates Bartimaeus's calling and approach; Matthew addresses two men.
Both requests ask for restored sight. Matthew's two men ask that their eyes be opened; Mark's blind man asks to see again.
Both conclude with immediate sight and following Jesus. Matthew includes compassion and touching two men's eyes; Mark emphasizes one man's faith and does not mention that touch.
Both place the approach to Jerusalem near Bethphage and the Mount of Olives and have Jesus send two disciples. Mark also names Bethany.
Both send disciples into the opposite village to untie and bring a mount. Matthew describes a donkey and her colt; Mark describes one tied colt on which nobody has sat.
Both supply the Lord's need as the answer to a challenge about taking the mount. Matthew uses the plural; Mark concerns one colt and mentions sending it back.
The fulfillment introduction leads into the following Zion-and-king quotation. Zechariah supplies the royal-mount oracle; the link reads Matthew's introduction together with 21:5.

Both present Zion's king as gentle and mounted on a beast of burden and colt. Matthew's introductory wording and animal description remain distinct rather than every clause being treated as verbatim repetition.
Matthew summarizes disciples obeying Jesus' directions; Mark narrates finding and untying the colt and answering as instructed. The accounts differ in the number of animals.
Both describe bringing the mount, placing garments upon it, and Jesus sitting upon it. Matthew includes donkey and colt; Mark narrates only the colt.
Both describe garments on the road and cut vegetation laid out for Jesus' arrival. Matthew specifies tree branches; Mark speaks of leafy branches cut from fields.
Both crowds cry Hosanna, bless the One coming in the Lord's name, and invoke Davidic kingship. Matthew names the Son of David; Mark names David's coming kingdom.
Both associate Jesus' kingship with a citywide Jerusalem reaction. The birth account describes Herod and Jerusalem troubled; the entry account describes the city shaken and asking His identity.
Both identify Jesus with Nazareth. Philip names Jesus son of Joseph from Nazareth; Matthew's crowd calls Him the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee. The speakers and occasions differ.
Both recount Jesus driving out temple buyers and sellers and overturning the money changers' tables and dove sellers' seats.
Both combine the house-of-prayer saying with the accusation of a robbers' den or cave. Mark explicitly includes for all the nations in the prayer-house clause.

Matthew narrates healing blind and lame people; Isaiah's restoration imagery promises opened blind eyes and a lame person leaping. This is a healing correspondence, not a claim Matthew explicitly quotes Isaiah here.

Both passages portray religious opponents objecting to praise of Jesus. Matthew describes chief priests and scribes indignant at children in the temple; Luke has Pharisees ask Jesus to rebuke disciples during the entry. This compares separate praise controversies without identifying them as the same exchange.
The words about prepared praise from infants and nursing children repeat distinctive wording of this edition's Greek-numbered Psalm 8:3. Jesus uses it to answer objections to the children's praise.

Both describe Jesus leaving Jerusalem for Bethany. Matthew places this departure after the temple cleansing and temple discussion, while Mark places his departure before his narrated cleansing. Matthew mentions staying the night; Mark mentions the Twelve. The shared travel details do not establish an identical immediate sequence.
Both begin the fig-tree episode with Jesus hungry as He travels from Bethany toward Jerusalem on the following morning or day.
Both have Jesus find a leafy fig tree without fruit and pronounce no future fruit. Matthew reports immediate withering; Mark's discovery of withering occurs later.
Both have disciples notice the cursed tree's withering. Matthew asks about its immediacy; Mark has Peter recall the curse when they pass the tree in the morning.
Both connect undoubting faith with commanding a mountain to be cast into the sea. Matthew explicitly connects the assurance with the fig tree.
Both associate believing prayer with receiving requests. Mark formulates it as believing that the requested things have already been received.
Both have religious authorities confront Jesus in the temple about His authority. Matthew mentions chief priests and elders; Mark also includes scribes.
Both answer the authority challenge by asking a prior question and making Jesus' answer conditional on their answering that question.
Both ask whether John's baptism came from heaven or humans and describe the authorities' reasoning that affirming heaven would invite a challenge about their failure to believe John.
Both describe fear of the crowd if the authorities call John's baptism human, because the people regard John as a prophet.
Both conclude with the authorities saying they do not know and Jesus consequently refusing to disclose the source of His own authority.
Both introduce a father and two children as a parable's framework. The plots differ: Matthew tests responses to a work command; Luke develops the younger son's departure and older son's response.
Both have a child's changed intention become actual movement. Luke's son resolves to return and rises and comes to his father; Matthew's first child reverses refusal and goes to work.
The second child gives respectful assent without acting; Luke challenges calling Jesus Lord while not doing what He says. Both distinguish verbal profession from action.

Matthew contrasts tax collectors entering ahead of the opponents with the obedient child. Luke likewise contrasts tax collectors responding to John's baptism with Pharisees and law experts rejecting God's purpose.
Both explicitly contrast tax collectors' positive response to John with the opponents' refusal. Matthew stresses belief and failure to change one's mind; Luke describes accepting or refusing baptism.
Both open the tenant parable with planting a vineyard, fencing it, digging a winepress, building a tower, leasing it, and traveling abroad.
Both have the owner send servants at fruit season to collect produce. Matthew's first mission is plural; Mark initially describes one slave.
Both describe tenants attacking the owner's messengers through beatings and killings. Matthew includes stoning and groups the initial slaves; Mark narrates successive individual attacks.
Both have further dispatched messengers meet continued violence. Matthew summarizes a larger second group; Mark describes individuals and many others.
Both make the owner's son the final messenger and give his hope that the tenants will respect him. Mark calls the son beloved.
Both have tenants identify the son as heir and conspire to kill him to obtain the inheritance.
Both narrate the son's seizure, death, and exclusion from the vineyard. Matthew places casting him outside before killing him; Mark places killing before throwing him outside.
Both ask what the owner will do after his son's death. Mark immediately supplies the answer in Jesus' telling; Matthew asks the listeners first.
Both answer that the owner destroys the tenants and gives the vineyard to others. Matthew specifies that the replacements will produce fruit in season.
Both quote the builders' rejected stone becoming the cornerstone and the Lord's marvelous action. Matthew gives the full quotation in one verse; Mark divides it into two.

Luke's vineyard parable describes transfer to others; Matthew explicitly applies transfer to the kingdom and a fruit-producing people. Luke's concrete wording does not itself name the kingdom or specify replacement ethnic groups.
Both say falling upon the stone shatters a person and the stone falling on someone crushes him. The two directions of the image correspond closely.
Both report the religious opponents recognizing that Jesus directed the parable against them. Mark connects that recognition with their wish to seize Him and fear of the crowd.
Both have opponents wanting to seize Jesus but restrained by fear of the crowd. Matthew additionally identifies the crowd's regard for Him as a prophet.
Both introduce a banquet parable connected with God's kingdom. Matthew again addresses opponents; Luke tells the story at a meal after a guest's kingdom remark.
Both picture a host preparing a great meal and inviting guests. Matthew specifies a king's wedding feast for his son; Luke names a man giving a great supper.
Both have a host summon previously invited people through a servant or servants, meeting refusal or excuses. Matthew says they were unwilling; Luke starts listing excuses.
Both invitations announce the meal's readiness and urge the invitees to come. Matthew includes slaughtered cattle and a renewed dispatch of slaves.
Both depict invited people preferring ordinary pursuits to the feast. Matthew gives field and business; Luke gives a field, oxen, and a new marriage.
The neighboring vineyard parable likewise has the master's messengers seized, mistreated, and killed. This same-book comparison concerns different parables, not the same group of historical victims.
Both parables depict rulers violently judging rejection of their rule or messengers. Matthew specifies troops and a burned city; Luke specifies execution before the ruler, without city-burning.
Both banquet stories exclude original invitees after their refusal. Matthew calls them unworthy; Luke says none of those invited men will taste the supper.
Both replace the original invitees by sending servants into streets or roads for new guests. Luke includes the poor and disabled and extends the search until the house is filled.

Both describe widened invitations intended to fill the banquet. Matthew explicitly gathers evil and good; Luke names marginalized people and people along roads without repeating those moral categories.
Both use exclusion into outer darkness with weeping and grinding of teeth as judgment imagery. Matthew 22 additionally describes binding the rejected guest's hands and feet.
Both introduce an attempt to trap Jesus in His speech. Matthew records Pharisees consulting; Mark records sending Pharisees and Herodians.
Both emissaries flatter Jesus as truthful, impartial, and a teacher of God's way. Matthew identifies Pharisaic disciples with Herodians as speakers.
Both ask whether giving tribute to Caesar is lawful. Mark continues with the explicit question whether they should give it or not.
Both have Jesus recognize hostile or hypocritical intent and challenge why they test Him. Matthew calls them hypocrites; Mark describes His knowledge of their hypocrisy.
Both have Jesus request a denarius and the questioners produce one. Matthew names the tribute coin; Mark asks for a denarius to inspect.
Both have Jesus ask whose image and inscription appear on the coin. Mark includes the reply Caesar's in the same verse.
Both identify the image as Caesar's and give the paired directive to return Caesar's things to Caesar and God's things to God.
Both report marveling at Jesus' tribute answer. Matthew adds that they leave Him and go away.
Both identify the Sadducees as denying resurrection and introduce their questioning. The comparison preserves the named group and stated doctrinal issue.
Both cite the Mosaic levirate premise: a childless man's brother should marry the widow and raise offspring for him.
Both begin with seven brothers, the first marrying and dying without offspring. Matthew explicitly says he left his wife to his brother.
Both extend the childless marriages through the other brothers, the second and third and eventually all seven. Mark repeats that none left offspring.
Both conclude the hypothetical case with the woman dying after the seven brothers. Mark includes the absence of offspring in the same verse.
Both ask whose wife the woman will be at the resurrection because all seven brothers had married her.
Both diagnose the Sadducees' error as ignorance of the Scriptures and God's power. Mark phrases it as a question.
Both say resurrected people neither marry nor are given in marriage and are like angels in heaven. Neither text says humans become angels.
Both introduce God's speech in Moses as evidence about resurrection. Mark identifies the burning-bush passage before quoting the patriarchal names.
Both cite God's identification with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and conclude that He is God of the living rather than the dead.
Matthew records the crowd's astonishment at Jesus' answer; Mark has a listening scribe recognize His good answer. These are different responses and speakers following the resurrection dispute.
Both move from the resurrection dispute to the foremost-commandment question. Matthew has Pharisees gather after the Sadducees' defeat; Mark focuses on a scribe impressed by Jesus' answer.
Both introduce a law-trained questioner. Matthew explicitly describes testing Jesus; Mark portrays a scribe recognizing His good answer without stating that testing motive.
Both ask which commandment ranks greatest or first, initiating the answer about love for God and neighbor.
Both require love of the Lord God with heart, soul, and mind. Mark also includes strength, absent from Matthew's supplied verse here.
Both identify love for God as the first or great commandment. Mark precedes it with the confession that the Lord is one.
Both identify loving one's neighbor as oneself as the second commandment. Mark immediately says none is greater than these.
Both give love of God and neighbor a governing rank. Matthew says the whole Law and Prophets hang on them; Mark says no commandment is greater.
Both introduce Jesus' own Christ-and-David question after the commandment discussion. Matthew specifies gathered Pharisees; Mark gives a temple teaching setting without naming those listeners here.
Both raise the claim that the Christ is David's son. Matthew asks whose son and records the answer; Mark asks how the scribes say He is David's son.
Both introduce David speaking in the Spirit and calling the addressed figure Lord before citing the enthronement psalm. Mark explicitly says Holy Spirit.
Matthew quotes the Lord commanding my lord to sit at His right until the enemies are beneath His feet. This edition numbers the psalm 109:1 and explicitly uses footstool imagery.
Both ask how the Christ can be David's son when David himself calls Him Lord. The question presses beyond simply stating Davidic descent.
Both say people no longer dared question Jesus. Matthew places the closure after the David-and-Lord question; Mark puts it before that teaching, preserving a difference in ordering.

deferred.reason: The fellow slaves' grief and report to the master were read. No sufficiently distinctive external counterpart was retained; general grief or reporting passages were not used merely to manufacture completion.

The disciples' inference that it would be better not to marry was read. General single-life teaching was considered, but no precise counterpart to this reaction to the divorce instruction was retained.
The third-hour marketplace hiring detail was read; no sufficiently precise independent counterpart was retained for this particular hiring round.
The sixth- and ninth-hour hiring rounds were read. Merely repeating adjacent narrative would not supply a sufficient counterpart for the distinctive details.
The eleventh-hour question about standing idle all day was read; no sufficiently precise counterpart to the time and question was retained.
The workers' explanation that nobody hired them and the resulting invitation were read; no precise external counterpart was retained.
The king's inspection and discovery of a guest without a wedding garment were read. General clothing imagery was not made into an unsupported identification of this garment.
The wedding-garment question and the guest's silence were read. No precise counterpart was retained, and no unsupported allegorical identification was supplied.
Many called but few chosen was read. General many/few sayings were considered imprecise for a retained pair. This sentence is not invented at Matthew20:16, where the pinned text does not contain it.

review_notes: All190 original source units in Matthew18–22 and every retained target passage were read from exact Saints snapshots. Source wording was not edited.
Matthew18 omits verse11. Mark9:43–45 contains consecutive original units v9-43 and v9-45; absent v9-44 was not invented.

Gospel differences remain explicit: mother versus sons making the request; two blind men versus Bartimaeus; donkey plus colt versus one colt; immediate withering versus later discovery; divorce qualifications; and the order of killing the son and casting him outside.

Same-chapter links in Matthew18 and20 identify mirrored petitions, contrasted debts or treatment, equal payments, or explicit callbacks to prior acts and contracts. They are internal literary comparisons, not independent corroboration.
Matthew20:1 to19:30 identifies the parable's first/last framing, repeated at20:16, and does not invent independent testimony to its unique hiring details.
Greek target numbering remains intact: Psalm8:3 for infant praise and Psalm109:1 for the enthronement quotation.
Matthew21:43 is not used to identify replacement ethnic groups beyond the text; Matthew22:30 is not described as humans becoming angels.
This is AI-assisted English passage review, not exhaustive concordance, Greek apparatus verification, independent human specialist approval, or live destination-anchor review.
